messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
The forward direction assumes M is complete and lets (F_n) satisfy the hypotheses.
Why is the chosen sequence Cauchy?
Choosing x_n in F_n gives d(x_n,x_m) <= diam F_n for m>n, so the diameters tending to 0 make (x_n) Cauchy and convergent to x in M, and each closed F_k contains the tail, so x lies in the intersection.
How does the intersection property force completeness?
Conversely, taking the closure of the tail of a Cauchy sequence (x_n) gives nonempty, closed, nested sets F_n whose diameters tend to 0, because closure does not increase diameter.
By hypothesis some x lies in all F_n, and since x_n and x both belong to F_n, the inequality d(x_n,x) <= diam F_n proves that x_n converges to x.
